subject: maths
title: Chance
seo_title: Year 5 Chance Worksheets: Outcomes, Equally Likely and Chance Experiments
standard_text: List the possible outcomes of chance experiments involving equally likely outcomes and compare to those which are not equally likely
meta_desc: Free Year 5 chance worksheets for the Australian Curriculum: list outcomes for coins, dice, spinners and marbles, decide if outcomes are equally likely, compare chances and use the results of repeated experiments. 100 maths questions with an answer key, great for NAPLAN practice.
key_big: List each outcome once, and look at the size of each part: bigger sections are more likely.
key_sub: Equal sections give equally likely outcomes. A coin or dice has no memory: after 5 heads, tails is still 1 out of 2. Many trials give a better estimate than a few.
body_html:
Outcomes

A chance experiment is something like tossing a coin, rolling a dice or spinning a spinner. An outcome is one thing that can happen. List each outcome once.

Example

A bag has 3 red marbles and 2 blue marbles. You take one. List the possible outcomes.

The marble can only be red or blue. Red is listed once, even though there are 3 red marbles.

Answer: red, blue

Equally likely or not?

Outcomes are equally likely when they have the same chance. On a spinner, look at the size of each colour, not just the number of colours.

Chance words

WordMeaningExample
certainwill happenrolling a number from 1 to 6
likelywill happen most of the timerolling more than 1
even chance1 out of 2a coin landing on heads
unlikelycan happen, but not oftenrolling a 6
impossiblecan never happenrolling a 7

Repeated experiments

Do an experiment many times and record the results in a frequency table. The outcome that comes up most is probably the most likely. More trials give a better estimate.

ColourFrequency (50 spins)
red26
blue12
yellow12
Which spinner?

The results above came from one spinner. Which one is it: equal thirds, or red half and blue and yellow a quarter each?

Red came up about half the time (26 of 50). Blue and yellow came up about a quarter of the time each.

Answer: red half, blue and yellow a quarter each

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
“3 colours, so each is 1 out of 3.”Look at the size of each section. Bigger sections are more likely.
“5 heads in a row, so tails is due.”A coin has no memory. Tails is still 1 out of 2.
Outcomes: red, red, blueList each outcome once: red, blue.
“6 rolls show 2 is the most likely.”Use many trials. A few results can be just luck.

faq.q: What do Year 5 students learn about chance in the Australian Curriculum?
faq.a: In Year 5 (AC9M5P01 and AC9M5P02) students list the possible outcomes of chance experiments, decide whether outcomes are equally likely, and run repeated experiments, using frequency to compare outcomes and estimate how likely they are.
Outcomes are equally likely when each has the same chance. A fair coin (heads or tails) and a spinner with equal sections are equally likely; a spinner where red covers half is not.

faq.q: If a coin lands on heads 5 times in a row, is tails more likely next?
faq.a: No. A fair coin has no memory, so tails is still 1 out of 2 on every toss. Thinking tails is “due” is a common mistake called the gambler’s fallacy.

faq.q: Why do more trials give a better estimate in a chance experiment?
faq.a: With only a few trials, luck can change the results a lot. With many trials (for example 50 or 100 spins) the frequencies get closer to the real chances, which is the kind of reasoning NAPLAN numeracy questions test.

items.q: You toss a coin. Which list shows all the possible outcomes?
items.e: A coin can land on heads or tails. List each outcome once. “1 out of 2” is the chance of one outcome, not a list of outcomes.

items.q: You roll a six-sided dice. How many possible outcomes are there?
items.e: The dice can land on 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6. That is 6 outcomes. There is no 0 on a dice, so not 7. Only one number comes up each roll, but there are 6 possible ones.

items.q: You roll a six-sided dice. Which number is NOT a possible outcome?
items.e: A dice shows 1 to 6. 7 can never come up.

items.q: Which list shows all the possible outcomes of this spinner?
items.e: The spinner can land on any of its 4 numbers: 1, 2, 3, 4. 5 is not on the spinner.

items.q: Which experiment has exactly 2 possible outcomes?
c: picking a day of the week
items.e: A coin has 2 outcomes: heads or tails. A dice has 6, the days of the week 7 and the spinner 4. So the answer is tossing a coin.

items.q: Which list shows all the possible outcomes of this spinner?
items.e: Red appears twice, but it is still only one outcome. List it once: red, blue, green.

items.q: A bag has 4 green and 4 white marbles. You take one without looking. How many different outcomes are there?
items.e: The outcome is a colour, so there are 2 outcomes: green or white. 8 is the number of marbles.

items.q: Cards numbered 1 to 10 are shuffled. You pick one card. How many possible outcomes are there?
items.e: Any card from 1 to 10 can be picked: that is 10 outcomes. There is no card 0, so not 11.

items.q: Which experiment has 7 possible outcomes?
c: picking a day of the week
picking a month of the year
items.e: There are 7 days in a week, so picking a day of the week has 7 outcomes. A dice has 6, the months 12 and a coin 2.

items.q: You roll a six-sided dice. Which list shows all the even outcomes?
items.e: The even numbers on a dice are 2, 4, 6. 1, 3, 5 are odd, and 8 is not on a dice.

items.q: You roll a six-sided dice. Which list shows all the outcomes greater than 4?
items.e: Greater than 4 means bigger than 4, so 4 is not included: 5, 6.

items.q: Which outcome is impossible on this spinner?
items.e: The numbers are 2, 4, 6 and 8. They are all even, so an odd number is impossible. 2 and 4 are less than 5, so that is possible.

items.q: Which list shows all the possible outcomes of this spinner?
items.e: Red is bigger, but it is still one outcome. Blue and yellow are possible too: red, blue, yellow. The size of a section changes the chance, not the list of outcomes.

items.q: A bag has 3 red, 2 blue and 1 yellow marble. You take one without looking. Which list shows all the possible outcomes?
c: red, red, red, blue, blue, yellow
items.e: The marble can be red, blue or yellow. Each colour is listed once: red, blue, yellow. Yellow is possible, even though there is only 1.

items.q: This spinner has 8 sections. How many different outcomes are there?
items.e: Count the different colours, not the sections: red, blue and green. That is 3 outcomes.

items.q: The letters of the word KOALA are written on 5 cards. You pick one card. Which list shows all the different possible outcomes?
items.e: KOALA has 5 letters, but A appears twice. The different outcomes are K, O, A, L.

items.q: Mia rolls a dice and gets a 6. Which list shows all the possible outcomes of her next roll?
items.e: The dice does not remember the last roll. All six numbers are possible again: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.

items.q: Which list shows all the outcomes on this spinner that are multiples of 3?
items.e: The multiples of 3 up to 8 are 3 and 6. 9 is a multiple of 3, but it is not on the spinner.

items.q: You toss a 10c coin and a 20c coin. H means heads and T means tails. Which list shows all the possible outcomes? (Write the 10c coin first.)
items.e: The 10c coin can be H or T, and so can the 20c coin. HT (10c heads, 20c tails) and TH (10c tails, 20c heads) are different. So there are 4: HH, HT, TH, TT.

items.q: A bag has 2 red, 1 blue and 1 green marble. Isla says the possible outcomes are “red, red, blue, green”. What is her mistake?
items.e: Each outcome is listed only once, so the list is red, blue, green. She listed red twice. There is no yellow marble.

items.q: Are the 4 colours on this spinner equally likely?
c: No, green is the least likely
No, red is at the top, so it is more likely
Yes, the 4 sections are the same size
items.e: Each colour has one quarter of the spinner. Equal sections give equally likely outcomes. Where a section is does not matter.

items.q: You toss a fair coin. Are heads and tails equally likely?
c: Only if you toss it twice
items.e: A fair coin has 2 outcomes with the same chance: heads 1 out of 2, tails 1 out of 2.

items.q: You roll a fair six-sided dice. Which statement is true?
c: Even numbers are more likely than odd
items.e: Each face has the same chance, 1 out of 6. So every number is equally likely. 6 feels hard to get only because people want it.

items.q: You take a marble without looking. Are red and blue equally likely?
items.e: There are 3 red and 3 blue marbles. The same number gives the same chance, so they are equally likely.

items.q: Are the outcomes on this spinner equally likely?
c: No, red has the biggest section
No, yellow has the biggest section
Yes, there are 3 colours, so each is the same
items.e: Red covers half the spinner. Blue and yellow cover a quarter each. So red is more likely. Having 3 colours does not make them equally likely.

items.q: You take a marble without looking. Are red and blue equally likely?
c: No, there are more red marbles
items.e: 5 red and 2 blue: red has more marbles, so red is more likely. Not equally likely. Two colours does not mean a 1 out of 2 chance each.

items.q: Are red and blue equally likely on this spinner?
c: Yes, each has 3 of the 6 sections
No, red is at the top
items.e: The 6 sections are the same size. Red has 3 and blue has 3, so they are equally likely.

items.q: Are red and blue equally likely on this spinner?
c: Yes, the sections are the same size
No, red has 4 of the 6 sections
items.e: The sections are equal, but red has 4 of them and blue only 2. So red is more likely: not equally likely.

items.q: You roll a six-sided dice. Is an even number equally likely as an odd number?
c: No, there are more even numbers
Yes, there are 3 even and 3 odd numbers
items.e: Even: 2, 4, 6. Odd: 1, 3, 5. Both have 3 outcomes, so they are equally likely.

items.q: You take a marble without looking. Which two colours are equally likely?
items.e: There are 4 green and 4 yellow marbles, so green and yellow are equally likely. Red has only 2.

items.q: Cards numbered 1 to 10 are shuffled. Is picking an even card equally likely as picking an odd card?
items.e: Even: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. Odd: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. Both have 5 cards, so they are equally likely.

items.q: A bag has 6 marbles: 2 red, 2 blue and 2 green. You take one without looking. Is each colour equally likely?
c: Yes, there are 2 of each colour
items.e: Each colour has 2 of the 6 marbles, so the colours are equally likely.

items.q: Which spinner has equally likely outcomes?
items.e: On spinner B red, blue and green each cover one third. On D the sections are equal, but red has 2 of them, so red is more likely.

items.q: Liam says each number on this spinner has a 1 out of 3 chance. Is he right?
items.e: 1 covers half of the spinner, but 2 and 3 only cover a quarter each. No: 1 is more likely than 2 or 3.

items.q: You roll a six-sided dice. Is rolling a 6 equally likely as rolling a number less than 6?
c: Yes, all dice numbers are equally likely
No, there are 5 numbers less than 6
items.e: Less than 6 means 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5: that is 5 outcomes. A 6 is only 1 outcome. So less than 6 is much more likely.

items.q: Are the 4 colours on this spinner equally likely?
c: No, the colours are split up
Yes, each has 2 of the 8 sections
items.e: The 8 sections are the same size, and each colour has 2 of them. So the colours are equally likely. Splitting a colour into two parts does not change its chance.

items.q: Which two colours on this spinner are equally likely?
items.e: Count the equal sections: red 3, blue 3, yellow 2. So red and blue are equally likely.

items.q: Which spinner does NOT have equally likely outcomes?
items.e: On spinner C the sections are different sizes: red is half, yellow is only one sixth. On D each colour has 2 of the 6 equal sections, so they are equally likely.

items.q: Are red and blue equally likely on this spinner?
c: No, red has 2 sections, so it is more likely
Yes, each covers a quarter of the spinner
No, red has small sections, so it is less likely
items.e: Red has two small sections, each one eighth. Together they make one quarter, the same as blue. So red and blue are equally likely. Compare the total size, not the number of pieces.

items.q: Charlotte wants a spinner where red, blue and yellow are equally likely. Which plan works?
c: red half, blue and yellow a quarter each
3 sections, each one third of the spinner
items.e: Equally likely colours need the same amount of the spinner. Three thirds works. Any size will not work: a big section is more likely.

items.q: You take a marble without looking. Which colour are you most likely to get?
items.e: There are 6 red, 3 blue and 1 yellow. Red has the most marbles, so red is most likely.

items.q: A bag has 2 red, 7 blue and 5 green marbles. You take one without looking. Which colour are you least likely to get?
items.e: Red has the fewest marbles (2), so red is least likely. Blue is the most likely.

items.q: Every section of a spinner is red. What is the chance it lands on red?
items.e: Red is the only colour, so the spinner must land on red. It is certain.

items.q: A bag has only red and blue marbles. What is the chance of taking a yellow marble?
items.e: There are no yellow marbles in the bag, so yellow is impossible.

items.q: A bag has 9 green marbles and 1 white marble. You take one without looking. What is the chance of green?
items.e: 9 of the 10 marbles are green, so green is likely. It is not certain, because you could take the white one.

items.q: What is the chance this spinner lands on blue?
items.e: Blue covers only one quarter. It can happen, but not often: unlikely. It is not impossible, because blue is on the spinner.

items.q: Which colour is this spinner most likely to land on?
items.e: Blue covers half the spinner, the biggest part. So blue is most likely. Red starts at the top, but that does not matter.

items.q: Which number is this spinner most likely to land on?
items.e: The 6 sections are equal. 1 has 1 section, 2 has 2 sections and 3 has 3 sections. So 3 is most likely.

items.q: Which statement about this spinner is true?
c: Red and blue are equally likely
Blue is more likely than red
Red is more likely than blue
items.e: Blue covers two thirds and red one third. So blue is more likely than red. Red is less likely, but not impossible.

items.q: Which colour is this spinner least likely to land on?
items.e: Count the equal sections: blue 3, yellow 3, red 2. Red has the least, so it is least likely.

items.q: You roll a six-sided dice. Which is more likely?
items.e: An even number can be 2, 4 or 6: 3 outcomes. A 6 is only 1 outcome. So an even number is more likely.

items.q: You roll a six-sided dice. Which is more likely?
items.e: Greater than 3: 4, 5, 6 (3 outcomes). Less than 3: 1, 2 (2 outcomes). The 3 itself is in neither list. So greater than 3 is more likely.

items.q: Cards numbered 1 to 10 are shuffled. You pick one. Which is more likely?
items.e: Even: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 (5 cards). Greater than 7: 8, 9, 10 (3 cards). So an even number is more likely.

items.q: Which spinner gives the best chance of landing on red?
items.e: Red covers three quarters of spinner D. That is more than half (A), one third (B) and one quarter (C).

items.q: On which spinner is blue least likely?
items.e: Blue is the smallest on spinner A: only one eighth of the spinner.

items.q: Bag A has 3 red and 1 blue marble. Bag B has 3 red and 3 blue marbles. You want a red marble. Which bag should you choose?
c: Both bags give the same chance
items.e: Both bags have 3 red, but in Bag A they are 3 out of 4 marbles and in Bag B only 3 out of 6. Bag A is better. Compare the red marbles with all the marbles.

items.q: Bag A has 2 red and 2 blue marbles. Bag B has 5 red and 5 blue marbles. You want a red marble. Which bag should you choose?
c: Both bags give the same chance
items.e: In both bags half the marbles are red. So the chance is the same: both bags give the same chance. Bag B has more red marbles, but it also has more blue ones.

items.q: Which is more likely on this spinner?
items.e: Less than 4: 1, 2, 3 (3 sections). Multiples of 4: 4, 8 (2 sections). So a number less than 4 is more likely.

items.q: A bag has 5 red, 2 blue and 3 green marbles. Which list orders the colours from least likely to most likely?
items.e: Order the counts from smallest: blue 2, green 3, red 5. So blue, green, red. “Red, green, blue” is most to least.

items.q: Kai says red is twice as likely as blue on this spinner. Is he right?
c: No, red is 3 times as likely
Yes, red’s part is twice as big
No, blue is twice as likely
items.e: Red is one half and blue is one quarter. Half is two quarters, so red’s part is twice as big. Kai is right.

items.q: Jack tosses a coin 20 times. He gets 11 heads and 9 tails. What does this show?
c: Heads is more likely next time
Heads and tails came up about the same
items.e: With a fair coin you expect about 10 of each, but rarely exactly 10. 11 and 9 are close, so heads and tails came up about the same.

items.q: A fair coin lands on heads 5 times in a row. What is the chance of tails on the next toss?
items.e: The coin does not remember earlier tosses. Every toss is still 1 out of 2 for tails. Tails is not “due”.

items.q: Leo has not rolled a 6 in his last 10 rolls of a fair dice. On his next roll, a 6 is…
items.e: Each roll is new. A 6 is 1 out of 6 every time, so it is just as likely as before.

items.q: Mei spins a red and blue spinner 40 times. Red comes up 21 times and blue the rest. How many times does blue come up?
items.e: 40 − 21 = 19. 61 comes from adding instead of subtracting.

items.q: Which colour probably has the biggest section on the spinner?
items.e: Red came up most often (14 of 25 spins), so red probably has the biggest section.

items.q: Which colour probably has the smallest section on the spinner?
items.e: Red came up least often (6 of 30 spins), so red probably has the smallest section.

items.q: What do these results suggest about the spinner?
c: Blue is the most likely colour
items.e: Blue came up 31 of 50 times, much more than red or yellow. So blue is probably the most likely colour. Yellow came up 10 times, so it is not impossible.

items.q: Which statement about these results is best?
c: 4 will come up more next time
5 is the most likely number on a dice
Each number came up about 10 times
items.e: 60 rolls ÷ 6 numbers = about 10 each. The results are all close to 10, so each number came up about 10 times. Small differences are normal.

items.q: You toss a fair coin 100 times. How many heads would you expect?
items.e: Heads is 1 out of 2, and half of 100 is 50. Results change each time, so expect about 50, not exactly 50.

items.q: You roll a fair dice 60 times. About how many times would you expect to roll a 3?
items.e: A 3 is 1 out of 6. 60 ÷ 6 = 10, so about 10. About 30 would be half the rolls.

items.q: A spinner is half red and half blue. You spin it 40 times. About how many times would you expect red?
items.e: Red is half of the spinner. Half of 40 is 20, so expect about 20.

items.q: You spin this spinner 20 times. About how many times would you expect blue?
items.e: Blue is one quarter of the spinner. 20 ÷ 4 = 5, so about 5. About 15 is for red. About 10 would only be right if blue were half.

items.q: You want to find out how likely red is on a spinner. Which gives the better estimate?
items.e: More spins give a better estimate. With only a few spins, luck changes the results a lot. So 100 spins is better.

items.q: Aarav spins a spinner 10 times and gets red 7 times. Zara spins the same spinner 200 times and gets red 104 times. Whose results tell you more about the spinner?
c: Aarav’s, because red came up more
items.e: 200 spins tell you much more than 10 spins. Zara’s results suggest red is about half the spinner.

items.q: Sienna rolls a dice 6 times and gets 2, 5, 2, 1, 2, 4. She says 2 is the most likely number on the dice. Is she right?
c: No, 6 rolls are too few to tell
items.e: On a fair dice every number is 1 out of 6. In only 6 rolls, some numbers come up more by luck. 6 rolls are too few to tell.

items.q: Ruby spins one of these spinners 50 times. Her results: red 26, blue 12, yellow 12. Which spinner did she most likely use?
items.e: Red came up about half the time (26 of 50). Blue and yellow came up about a quarter of the time each. That matches spinner B: red half, blue and yellow a quarter each.

items.q: Oliver spins one of these spinners 50 times. His results: red 17, blue 16, yellow 17. Which spinner did he most likely use?
items.e: The three colours came up about the same number of times. So the colours are probably equally likely: spinner C, with three equal thirds.

items.q: Chloe spins one of these spinners 50 times. Her results: red 38, blue 12. Which spinner did she most likely use?
items.e: Red came up much more often than blue: about 3 times as often. Spinner D is three quarters red. On B, blue would win most of the time.

items.q: Noah spins one of these spinners 50 times. His results: red 5, blue 24, yellow 21. Which spinner did he most likely use?
items.e: Red came up only 5 times, so red is probably small. Blue came up about half the time. That matches spinner A: red one eighth, blue half, yellow a bit less than half.

items.q: A bag has 10 red and blue marbles. Cooper takes one, writes the colour and puts it back. He does this 50 times: red 39, blue 11. What is most likely in the bag?
items.e: Red came up about 4 times as often as blue. 8 red and 2 blue fits: red is 4 times as likely. 8 red, 2 blue. It can’t be 10 red, because blue came up 11 times.

items.q: Before a cricket match the captains toss a coin. One captain calls “heads”. Which words best describe the chance the call is right?
items.e: Heads and tails are equally likely, 1 out of 2. That is an even chance.

items.q: The school fete raffle sells 100 tickets. Charlotte buys 1 ticket. One ticket wins. What is her chance of winning?
items.e: 1 of the 100 tickets is hers, so her chance is 1 out of 100. “Win or lose” is not 1 out of 2, because losing is much more likely.

items.q: The same raffle has 100 tickets. Matilda buys 5 tickets. What is her chance of winning?
items.e: 5 of the 100 tickets are hers, so her chance is 5 out of 100. More tickets give a better chance.

items.q: A Year 5 class has 25 students. The teacher picks one name from a hat. What is the chance that Ethan is picked?
items.e: Ethan’s name is 1 of the 25 names, so the chance is 1 out of 25. 24 out of 25 is the chance he is NOT picked.

items.q: A lucky dip at the school fete has 20 prizes. 4 of them are toy koalas. Grace takes one without looking. What is her chance of a toy koala?
items.e: 4 of the 20 prizes are koalas: 4 out of 20. Compare with all 20 prizes, not with the 16 others. 16 out of 20 is the chance of NOT a koala.

items.q: A netball team has 7 bibs: GS, GA, WA, C, WD, GD and GK. Isla takes one bib without looking. What is the chance she gets C?
items.e: There are 7 bibs and 1 of them is C, so the chance is 1 out of 7. 6 out of 7 is the chance of not C.

items.q: In a board game, Noah needs to roll a 5 or a 6 to win. What is his chance?
items.e: 2 numbers (5 and 6) out of the 6 numbers on a dice: 2 out of 6.

items.q: Amelia needs to roll more than 1 on a dice to move her counter. Which word best describes her chance?
items.e: More than 1 means 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6: 5 out of 6. That is likely, but not certain, because she could roll a 1.

items.q: A jar has 12 lollies: 6 orange, 4 lime and 2 lemon. Kai takes one without looking. Which flavour is he least likely to get?
items.e: Lemon has the fewest lollies (2), so lemon is least likely.

items.q: A spinner game at the school fair has 8 equal sections. One says WIN. What is the chance of winning on one spin?
items.e: 1 of the 8 equal sections is WIN, so the chance is 1 out of 8.

items.q: The jar has 6 orange, 4 lime and 2 lemon lollies. What is the chance of an orange lolly?
items.e: 6 of the 12 lollies are orange: 6 out of 12, an even chance. 1 out of 3 would only be right if the 3 flavours were equally likely.

items.q: Sienna picks a day of the week at random. What is the chance it is Saturday or Sunday?
items.e: There are 7 days and 2 of them are on the weekend: 2 out of 7. 2 out of 5 compares the weekend with the 5 school days, not with all 7.

items.q: A class has 13 girls and 12 boys. One name is picked from a hat. Is a girl more likely than a boy?
c: No, a boy is more likely
items.e: 13 girls and 12 boys: a girl is a little more likely. Yes, but only a little. It is not certain.

items.q: Harper tosses a coin. It lands on tails 6 times in a row. She says, “Heads must come next.” Is she right?
c: No, tails is more likely now
No, heads is still 1 out of 2
items.e: Each toss is new and the coin does not remember. Heads is still 1 out of 2.

items.q: A special dice has the numbers 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3 on its faces. What is the chance of rolling a 3?
items.e: Two of the 6 faces show a 3, so the chance is 2 out of 6. 3 out of 6 comes from using the number 3 instead of counting faces.

items.q: The school canteen has a box of 30 muffins: 10 blueberry and 20 chocolate. Mia takes one without looking. Which statement is true?
c: Blueberry is more likely than chocolate
Chocolate is more likely than blueberry
items.e: There are 20 chocolate and only 10 blueberry, so chocolate is more likely. It is not certain, because there are blueberry muffins too.

items.q: Ava makes a spinner with 4 equal parts. She wants red to be likely and blue to be unlikely. Which plan works?
items.e: 3 red and 1 blue makes red likely and blue unlikely. With 0 blue parts, blue would be impossible.

items.q: At the athletics carnival, tickets numbered 1 to 30 go in a hat for a prize. Which is more likely: a number from 1 to 10, or a number from 21 to 30?
items.e: Each group has 10 tickets, and every ticket has the same chance. So they are equally likely. Bigger numbers are not harder to pick.

items.q: A bag has 3 red marbles and some blue marbles. Red and blue are equally likely. How many blue marbles are there?
items.e: Equally likely means the same number of each colour. So there are 3 blue marbles.

items.q: A bag has 2 green and 3 yellow marbles. William wants green to be MORE likely than yellow. What is the smallest number of green marbles he must add?
items.e: Add 1: 3 green and 3 yellow are only equally likely. Add 2: 4 green beats 3 yellow.
